title: Halogen compounds
objectives: Recall ways of making halogenoalkanes: free-radical substitution of alkanes, electrophilic addition of HX or X₂ to alkenes, and substitution of alcohols (HX, KCl/NaBr with concentrated H₂SO₄, PCl₃/PCl₅/SOCl₂, PBr₃, PI₃)
Classify halogenoalkanes as primary, secondary or tertiary
Describe nucleophilic substitution with NaOH(aq), KCN in ethanol and NH₃ in ethanol, and hydrolysis by water with AgNO₃
Describe and explain the SN1 and SN2 mechanisms, and which halogenoalkanes react by each
Explain the relative reactivity of C–Cl, C–Br and C–I in terms of bond strength
Describe elimination of HX using NaOH in ethanol to form alkenes, and count the alkenes (including E/Z) that can form
prior: Mechanism vocabulary: nucleophile, heterolytic fission, curly arrows (Chapter 13)
why: Halogenoalkanes are the 'switching station' of organic synthesis: one halogen atom can be swapped for OH, CN or NH₂, or removed to give an alkene. They also give you the two substitution mechanisms, SN1 and SN2, which Paper 2 asks you to draw.
intro: A halogenoalkane has a halogen atom bonded to an sp³ carbon. The halogen is more electronegative than carbon, so the C–X bond is polar (Cδ+–Xδ−). The δ+ carbon attracts nucleophiles, and X⁻ is a good leaving group.

blocks.h: Count the carbon atoms bonded to the carbon that carries the halogen: one → primary (1-bromobutane), two → secondary (2-bromobutane), three → tertiary (2-bromo-2-methylpropane). This decides the mechanism of substitution.

reagent and conditions
example
rows: Cl₂ or Br₂, UV light (free-radical substitution)
CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl (mixture of products)
HX, or KCl / NaBr with concentrated H₂SO₄ (makes HX in the flask), heat
PBr₃ or PI₃ (made from red P and Br₂ or I₂), warm

blocks.wrong: Halogen water (e.g. Br₂(aq)) turns an alcohol into a halogenoalkane.
blocks.right: The OH group has to be replaced by a halide using HX or a phosphorus/sulfur halide. Bromine water reacts with C=C, not with an alcohol.

blocks.h: A nucleophile (OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃, H₂O) donates a lone pair to the δ+ carbon. The C–X bond breaks heterolytically: both electrons go to X, which leaves as X⁻.

items: One step. A curly arrow goes from the lone pair on OH⁻ to the δ+ C, and another from the C–X bond to X.
The nucleophile attacks from the side opposite X. In the transition state the C–OH bond is half made and the C–X bond half broken; it carries a negative charge spread over both ends: [HO···C···Br]⁻.
Rate depends on both species: Substitution, Nucleophilic, 2 species in the rate-determining step.
Step 1 (slow): C–X breaks on its own, giving a carbocation and X⁻: (CH₃)₃C–Br → (CH₃)₃C⁺ + Br⁻.
Step 2 (fast): the nucleophile's lone pair attacks C⁺: (CH₃)₃C⁺ + OH⁻ → (CH₃)₃COH.
Only 1 species in the rate-determining step. The energy profile has two peaks, the first higher, with the carbocation in the dip between them.

head: primary
tertiary
rows: tertiary C⁺ stabilised by three electron-donating alkyl groups
open: easy for a nucleophile to attack from behind
crowded by three alkyl groups (steric hindrance)

blocks.title: Halogenoalkane reaction explorer
blocks.h: Pick a halogenoalkane and a reagent to see the product, the type of reaction and the mechanism.

blocks.wrong: In SN1 the hydroxide ion attacks in the first step.
blocks.right: In SN1 the first (slow) step involves the halogenoalkane only. The nucleophile only reacts once the carbocation has formed.

sections.title: Reactivity: C–Cl, C–Br, C–I and the silver nitrate test

blocks.h: Warm a halogenoalkane with AgNO₃ in aqueous ethanol. Water slowly substitutes the halogen; the X⁻ released forms a precipitate with Ag⁺. The time taken for cloudiness measures the rate.

C–Cl is the most polar bond, so polarity alone would predict the chloro compound reacts fastest. It does not: the C–X bond must break, and the weakest bond (C–I) breaks most easily. Bond energy, not polarity, decides.

blocks.name: agrace
blocks.title: Silver nitrate race
blocks.h: Compare how quickly different halogenoalkanes give a precipitate.

blocks.q: Put 1-bromobutane, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane and 1-chlorobutane in order of rate with warm aqueous AgNO₃, fastest first.
steps: compare halogens: C–Br is weaker than C–Cl, so both bromo compounds beat 1-chlorobutane
compare the bromo compounds: the tertiary one ionises (SN1) to a stable carbocation and reacts faster
blocks.err: Explaining the order by electronegativity or polarity of C–X.

product
example from 1-bromopropane
rows: KCN in ethanol, heat under reflux
excess NH₃ in ethanol, heated in a sealed tube (under pressure)

items: KCN supplies CN⁻. Ethanol is the solvent because water would also act as a nucleophile and give the alcohol.
Name the nitrile by counting the carbon of C≡N: bromoethane gives propanenitrile.
With NH₃, the amine product can react further with more halogenoalkane; excess NH₃ keeps this to a minimum. Overall: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + 2NH₃ → CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂ + NH₄Br.

blocks.right: CN adds a carbon atom: CH₃CH₂CN has three carbons, so it is propanenitrile.

blocks.h: With NaOH (or KOH) dissolved in ethanol, heated under reflux, OH⁻ acts as a base. It removes an H⁺ from a carbon next to the C–X carbon; X⁻ leaves and a C=C forms. Overall HX is eliminated: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + NaOH → CH₃CH=CH₂ + NaBr + H₂O.

items: List each carbon next to C–X that carries an H; each can give a different C=C.
Check each alkene for E/Z isomers (both C=C carbons must carry two different groups).
A carbon next to C–X with no H (e.g. in (CH₃)₃CCH₂Br) cannot take part, and that compound cannot eliminate at all.

blocks.q: How many alkenes (including stereoisomers) form when 2-bromo-3-methylbutane, CH₃CHBrCH(CH₃)₂, is heated with ethanolic KOH?
steps: H lost from C1 → CH₂=CHCH(CH₃)₂, 3-methylbut-1-ene (no E/Z)
H lost from C3 → CH₃CH=C(CH₃)₂, 2-methylbut-2-ene (no E/Z: C3 has two CH₃)
blocks.err: Assuming every internal C=C has E/Z isomers.

summary: C–X is polar (Cδ+); nucleophiles attack the δ+ carbon and X⁻ leaves (heterolytic fission).
Make halogenoalkanes from alkanes (X₂/UV), alkenes (HX or X₂) or alcohols (HX, NaBr/KCl + conc. H₂SO₄, PCl₅, PCl₃, SOCl₂, PBr₃, PI₃).
NaOH(aq) → alcohol; KCN in ethanol → nitrile (+1 C); excess NH₃ in ethanol, sealed tube → amine.
Primary → SN2 (one step, transition state). Tertiary → SN1 (C⁺ intermediate; slow step involves one species). Secondary → both.
Tertiary carbocations are stabilised by electron-donating alkyl groups.
Rate: C–I > C–Br > C–Cl because bond strength decreases; polarity does not explain the order.
AgNO₃ test: white AgCl, cream AgBr, yellow AgI.
NaOH in ethanol, hot → elimination of HX to an alkene; count alkenes including E/Z.

practice.q: Describe the SN2 mechanism for 1-bromopropane with hydroxide ions.
practice.a: C–Br dipole; curly arrow from a lone pair on OH⁻ to δ+ C; curly arrow from C–Br bond to Br; transition state [HO···C···Br]⁻; products propan-1-ol and Br⁻.

practice.q: Describe the SN1 mechanism for 2-bromo-2-methylpropane with hydroxide ions.
practice.a: Curly arrow from C–Br bond to Br (slow) giving (CH₃)₃C⁺ + Br⁻; curly arrow from lone pair on OH⁻ to C⁺ (fast) giving (CH₃)₃COH.

practice.q: Explain why 1-iodobutane is hydrolysed faster than 1-chlorobutane.
practice.a: The C–I bond is weaker (lower bond energy) than C–Cl, so it breaks more easily; this outweighs C–Cl being more polar.

practice.q: Give the reagents, conditions and product to make butanenitrile from a halogenoalkane.
practice.a: 1-bromopropane (or 1-chloropropane) with KCN in ethanol, heated under reflux; CH₃CH₂CH₂CN.

practice.q: Name all the alkenes formed when 2-bromopentane is heated with ethanolic NaOH.

practice.a: Warm with AgNO₃ in aqueous ethanol: 1-iodobutane gives a yellow precipitate quickly; 1-chlorobutane gives a white precipitate slowly.

assessment_s.q:
1-bromobutane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane are isomers, C₄H₉Br.
(a) Classify each as primary, secondary or tertiary. [1]
(b) Each is warmed with NaOH(aq). Name the mechanism for each and describe the mechanism for 1-bromobutane. [4]
(c) Which isomer reacts faster with warm aqueous AgNO₃? Explain. [2]
assessment_s.a:
(a) 1-bromobutane primary; 2-bromo-2-methylpropane tertiary
(b) 1-bromobutane SN2; 2-bromo-2-methylpropane SN1. SN2: lone pair on OH⁻ attacks δ+ C; C–Br bond breaks heterolytically to Br⁻; transition state [HO···C···Br]⁻; butan-1-ol formed
(c) 2-bromo-2-methylpropane; it forms a tertiary carbocation, which is stabilised by three electron-donating alkyl groups

assessment_s.q:
2-chloropentane is heated with KOH dissolved in ethanol.
(a) Name the type of reaction and the role of OH⁻. [2]
(b) Name all the organic products, including stereoisomers. [2]
(c) Give the reagent and conditions to turn 2-chloropentane into 2-methylpentanenitrile. [2]
assessment_s.a:
(a) elimination; base
(b) pent-1-ene, (E)-pent-2-ene, (Z)-pent-2-ene
(c) KCN in ethanol, heat under reflux

pp.skill: Which halogenoalkanes form when an alkene meets HX
pp.mis: Thinking the two hydrogen halides add together across one C=C
pp.stem:
But-1-ene is reacted with a mixture of HCl(g) and HBr(g). Three compounds are listed.
1 1-chlorobutane
2 2-bromobutane
3 2-bromo-1-chlorobutane
Which could be formed?
pp.exp: Each C=C adds one H–X. HCl gives 2-chlorobutane (major) and 1-chlorobutane (minor); HBr gives 2-bromobutane (major) and 1-bromobutane (minor). Compound 3 would need Br and Cl to add together, which needs BrCl, not HX.

pp.skill: Reagents that turn an alcohol into a halogenoalkane
pp.mis: Thinking the halogen itself substitutes for OH
pp.stem:
Three reagents are listed.
1 PBr₃ (made from red phosphorus and bromine), warmed
2 bromine water at room temperature
3 NaBr(s) with concentrated H₂SO₄, heated
Which convert propan-1-ol into 1-bromopropane?
pp.exp: PBr₃ replaces OH with Br. NaBr + conc. H₂SO₄ makes HBr in the flask, which substitutes the OH. Bromine water does not react with an alcohol.

pp.skill: Moving a halogen to a different carbon via an alkene
pp.mis: Choosing a direct substitution that keeps the halogen on C1
pp.stem: Which reagents, used in order, could make 2-chloropropane from propan-1-ol?
pp.exp: Dehydration gives propene; adding HCl then gives mainly 2-chloropropane (via the secondary carbocation). PCl₅ and NaCl/H₂SO₄ give 1-chloropropane; Cl₂/UV gives a mixture of substitution products of an alkane, not this.

pp.skill: Naming the reaction types in a two-step route
pp.mis: Mixing up elimination and substitution
pp.stem:
2-bromo-2-methylpropane is converted into 1,2-dibromo-2-methylpropane in two reactions.
reaction 1: heat with NaOH in ethanol
reaction 2: add Br₂ at room temperature
Which types of reaction are these?
pp.exp: Ethanolic NaOH removes HBr to give methylpropene (elimination). Br₂ then adds across the C=C (electrophilic addition), giving (CH₃)₂CBrCH₂Br.

pp.skill: Nature of the attacking group and leaving group
pp.mis: Calling the leaving halide an electrophile
pp.stem: 1-iodobutane reacts with aqueous KOH to form butan-1-ol. What are the attacking group and the leaving group?
opts: OH⁻, a nucleophile; I⁻, a nucleophile
OH⁻, an electrophile; I⁻, a nucleophile
OH⁻, a nucleophile; I⁻, an electrophile
K⁺, an electrophile; I⁻, a nucleophile
pp.exp: OH⁻ donates a lone pair to the δ+ carbon, so it is a nucleophile. I⁻ leaves taking the bonding pair; it has lone pairs it could donate, so it is also a nucleophile.

pp.skill: Which species meet in the first step of SN1 and SN2
pp.mis: Thinking OH⁻ attacks the tertiary compound in step 1
pp.stem: R is either a primary or a tertiary bromoalkane. It is hydrolysed by aqueous NaOH. In the first step of the mechanism, two species react together. Which is correct?
opts: R is tertiary; OH⁻ acts as a nucleophile
R is primary; OH⁻ acts as an electrophile
R is primary; OH⁻ acts as a nucleophile
R is tertiary; OH⁻ acts as an electrophile
pp.exp: A primary bromoalkane reacts by SN2: the first (only) step is OH⁻ attacking the δ+ carbon. A tertiary one reacts by SN1, whose first step involves one species only: C–Br breaks on its own.

pp.skill: Drawing the first curly arrow in SN2
pp.mis: Starting the arrow from the carbon instead of the lone pair
pp.stem: A student draws the SN2 mechanism for chloroethane turning into ethanol with hydroxide ions. Where should the arrow that represents the attack begin and end?
opts: begin at an O lone pair of the hydroxide ion; end at the δ+ C
begin at the δ+ C; end at the hydroxide ion
begin at the C–Cl bond; end at the C
no arrow: the C–Cl bond splits into two radicals
pp.exp: Curly arrows start at an electron pair. The OH⁻ lone pair moves to the δ+ C, while a second arrow moves the C–Cl bonding pair onto Cl (heterolytic fission).

pp.skill: Features of the SN2 mechanism
pp.mis: Thinking a carbocation forms for a primary compound
pp.stem: 1-bromopropane is warmed with KOH(aq). Which description of its mechanism is right?
opts: OH⁻ bonds to the δ+ C in the same step as Br⁻ leaves
Br⁻ leaves first; OH⁻ then bonds to a carbocation
C–Br splits into radicals; OH• then bonds to the propyl radical
K⁺ attacks the δ− Br, then OH⁻ bonds to the carbon
pp.exp: 1-bromopropane is primary, so it reacts by SN2: OH⁻ attacks the δ+ C as C–Br breaks heterolytically, in one step with no carbocation.

pp.skill: The SN2 transition state
pp.mis: Choosing a carbocation for a primary halogenoalkane
pp.stem: 1-bromobutane reacts with KCN in ethanol by nucleophilic substitution. What is the most likely species formed part-way through the reaction?
opts: a transition state with partial bonds NC···C···Br and an overall negative charge
pp.exp: Primary halogenoalkanes react by SN2. In the transition state the C–CN bond is forming as the C–Br bond is breaking; the single negative charge is spread over CN and Br.

pp.skill: Features of the SN1 mechanism
pp.mis: Thinking the SN1 intermediate is neutral
pp.stem: Which statement about the SN1 mechanism of a halogenoalkane is correct?
opts: Its rate-determining step involves two species.
Alkyl groups around the positive carbon make the intermediate more stable.
A free radical is formed when the C–X bond breaks.
pp.exp: In SN1 the C–X bond breaks first (one species, slow) to give a carbocation. Alkyl groups donate electron density (positive inductive effect), stabilising C⁺, which is why tertiary compounds react this way.

pp.skill: Carbocation stability and halogenoalkane reactions
pp.mis: Thinking chloroalkanes react faster than bromoalkanes
pp.stem: Which statement is correct?
opts: Chloroethane forms ethene as the major product with NaOH(aq).
1-chloropropane is hydrolysed faster than 1-iodopropane at the same temperature.
Hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylbutane takes place mainly by SN2.
The (CH₃)₂C⁺CH₂CH₃ ion is more stable than the CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂C⁺H₂ ion.
pp.exp: A tertiary carbocation has three electron-donating alkyl groups, so it is more stable than a primary one. NaOH(aq) gives substitution; C–Cl is stronger than C–I so is slower; tertiary compounds react mainly by SN1.

pp.skill: Energy profile for a two-step SN1 reaction
pp.mis: Drawing one hump for a two-step reaction
pp.stem:
The exothermic hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane occurs in two steps.
step 1 (slow): (CH₃)₃C–Br → (CH₃)₃C⁺ + Br⁻
step 2 (fast): (CH₃)₃C⁺ + OH⁻ → (CH₃)₃C–OH
Which describes the reaction pathway diagram?
opts: one peak; products lower than reactants
two peaks, the first higher; a dip between them; products lower than reactants
two peaks, the second higher; a dip between them; products lower than reactants
two peaks, the first higher; a dip between them; products higher than reactants
pp.exp: Two steps give two transition states (peaks) with the carbocation intermediate in the dip. The slow step has the larger activation energy, so the first peak is higher. Exothermic means products end below reactants.

pp.skill: Order of hydrolysis rates with silver nitrate
pp.mis: Explaining the rate by bond polarity
pp.stem: A few drops each of 2-chloropropane, 2-bromopropane and 2-iodopropane are added to separate tubes of warm aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol. Which shows the order in which a precipitate first appears, and the reason?
opts: chloro, bromo, iodo; C–Cl is the most polar bond
iodo, bromo, chloro; C–I is the weakest bond
iodo, bromo, chloro; C–I is the most polar bond
chloro, bromo, iodo; C–Cl is the strongest bond
pp.exp: The rate depends on how easily C–X breaks. C–I has the lowest bond energy, so 2-iodopropane gives its (yellow) precipitate first. Polarity predicts the opposite order, so it is not the deciding factor.

pp.skill: Comparing rates: bond energy, not polarity
pp.mis: Choosing bond polarity as the explanation
pp.stem: 1-chloropropane and 1-iodopropane react separately with aqueous NaOH under the same conditions. Which is correct?
opts: 1-chloropropane reacts faster; the C–Cl bond is more polar
1-chloropropane reacts faster; chlorine is more electronegative
1-iodopropane reacts faster; the C–I bond is weaker
1-iodopropane reacts faster; iodine is more reactive than chlorine
pp.exp: Breaking C–X is needed in the mechanism. C–I (about 240 kJ mol⁻¹) is much weaker than C–Cl (about 340 kJ mol⁻¹), so the iodo compound reacts faster.

pp.skill: Fastest reaction and its mechanism
pp.mis: Pairing a tertiary compound with SN2
pp.stem: 2-chloro-2-methylpropane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane each react with aqueous NaOH. Which reaction is faster under the same conditions, and by which mechanism?
pp.exp: Both are tertiary, so they react by SN1. C–Br is weaker than C–Cl, so the bromo compound forms its carbocation faster.

pp.skill: Combining structure and halogen to compare rates
pp.mis: Looking only at the halogen and ignoring primary/tertiary
pp.stem: 1-chlorobutane and 2-iodo-2-methylpropane react separately with aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol under the same conditions. The time for a precipitate to appear is t₁ for 1-chlorobutane and t₂ for 2-iodo-2-methylpropane. Which is correct?
opts: t₁ < t₂; the precipitate for 2-iodo-2-methylpropane is white
t₁ > t₂; the precipitate for 2-iodo-2-methylpropane is yellow
t₁ > t₂; the precipitate for 2-iodo-2-methylpropane is cream
t₁ = t₂; both precipitates are yellow
pp.exp: 2-iodo-2-methylpropane has the weakest C–X bond and is tertiary (SN1 via a stable carbocation), so it reacts much faster: t₂ is shorter. AgI is yellow; AgCl (from 1-chlorobutane, slowly) is white.

pp.skill: Explaining rate differences in tertiary hydrolysis
pp.mis: Explaining by electronegativity
pp.stem: (CH₃)₃C–X + H₂O → (CH₃)₃C–OH + HX, where X is Br or Cl. Which statement is correct?
opts: The reaction is faster when X is Br because the C–Br bond is weaker than the C–Cl bond.
The reaction is faster when X is Cl because the C–Cl bond is more polar.
The reaction mainly follows SN2 because water is a weak nucleophile.
The rate-determining step involves both water and the halogenoalkane.
pp.exp: Tertiary compounds react by SN1; the slow step is breaking C–X alone. The weaker C–Br bond breaks more easily, so X = Br is faster.

pp.skill: Matching mechanism and precipitate colour
pp.mis: Mixing up the silver halide colours
pp.stem: Which halogenoalkane reacts with water mainly by an SN2 mechanism and gives a cream precipitate when aqueous AgNO₃ is added?
pp.exp: Primary → SN2. Cream AgBr shows bromine. 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is tertiary (SN1); chloro gives white AgCl and iodo gives yellow AgI.

pp.skill: Identifying a halogenoalkane from two tests
pp.mis: Forgetting that elimination needs an H on the next carbon
pp.stem: When Y is warmed with AgNO₃ in aqueous ethanol a white solid forms, and this solid dissolves in dilute NH₃(aq). Hot ethanolic KOH turns Y into an alkene. Which could be Y?
pp.exp: Soluble in dilute NH₃ means AgCl, so Y is a chloroalkane. In (CH₃)₃CCH₂Cl the carbon next to C–Cl has no H, so it cannot eliminate; 2-chloropropane can, giving propene.

pp.skill: Recognising an SN2 reaction
pp.mis: Treating elimination with ethanolic KOH as substitution
pp.stem: Which reaction is classified as SN2?
pp.exp: A primary halogenoalkane with a nucleophile in aqueous solution reacts by SN2. Tertiary compounds (A, D) react by SN1; hot ethanolic KOH (C) causes elimination.

pp.skill: Reaction type from the conditions
pp.mis: Calling it SN1 because OH⁻ is involved
pp.stem: How is the reaction of 1-chloropropane with warm NaOH(aq) best described?
opts: substitution in which an electrophile replaces Cl
loss of HCl to form propene
one-step attack by OH⁻ as Cl⁻ leaves (SN2)
loss of Cl⁻ to form a carbocation first (SN1)
pp.exp: Aqueous NaOH favours substitution. 1-chloropropane is primary, so the mechanism is SN2 (a primary carbocation would be too unstable for SN1).

pp.skill: Percentage yield and rate comparison
pp.mis: Using the mass of the halogenoalkane as the theoretical mass
pp.stem:
Two reactions, under identical conditions with excess NaOH(aq):
1 2-iodo-2-methylpropane
2 2-chloro-2-methylpropane
In reaction 1, 36.80 g of 2-iodo-2-methylpropane gives 11.12 g of 2-methylpropan-2-ol. [Mr: C₄H₉I, 184.0; C₄H₁₀O, 74.12]
Which is correct?
pp.exp: n = 36.80 ÷ 184.0 = 0.2000 mol, so the maximum mass of product = 0.2000 × 74.12 = 14.82 g. Yield = 11.12 ÷ 14.82 × 100 = 75.0%. C–I is weaker than C–Cl, so reaction 1 is faster. (11.12 ÷ 36.80 = 30.2% wrongly compares masses.)

pp.skill: Reagent and conditions to make a nitrile
pp.mis: Choosing HCN or an acid solvent
pp.stem: CH₃CH₂Cl + CN⁻ → CH₃CH₂CN + Cl⁻ lengthens the carbon chain. Which reagent and conditions are used?
opts: HCN, heat under reflux in ethanol
KCN, heat under reflux in water with dilute acid
KCN, heat under reflux in ethanol
pp.exp: KCN supplies CN⁻ ions. It is heated under reflux in ethanol: water would compete as a nucleophile (giving the alcohol), and acid would turn CN⁻ into HCN.

pp.skill: Choosing the halogenoalkane to make a given nitrile
pp.mis: Forgetting that CN adds a carbon atom
pp.stem: Which gives hexanenitrile, CH₃(CH₂)₄CN, as a product?
pp.exp: Hexanenitrile has six carbons including the C of CN. The halogenoalkane must therefore have five: 1-bromopentane, with KCN in ethanol.

pp.skill: Product with KCN from the same halogenoalkane
pp.mis: Putting the CN on the end carbon
pp.stem: When X is heated under reflux with NaOH(aq), butan-2-ol is formed. What is formed when X is heated with KCN in ethanol?
pp.exp: X is a 2-halobutane. CN⁻ replaces the halogen on C2, giving CH₃CH₂CH(CN)CH₃. Numbering from the nitrile carbon, this is 2-methylbutanenitrile.

pp.skill: Mass of nitrile from a percentage yield
pp.mis: Naming the nitrile from the halogenoalkane carbon count
pp.stem:
49.2 g of 1-bromopropane is heated with excess KCN in ethanol. The yield of the organic product is 65.0%. [Mr: C₃H₇Br, 123.0; C₄H₇N, 69.0]
Which is correct?
pp.exp: n = 49.2 ÷ 123.0 = 0.400 mol → 0.400 mol C₃H₇CN (4 C: butanenitrile). Maximum mass 0.400 × 69.0 = 27.6 g; 65.0% of this is 17.9 g.

pp.skill: Which reaction mixture forms an amine
pp.mis: Thinking KCN makes an amine directly
pp.stem: Which reaction mixture produces a primary amine?
opts: halogenoalkane heated with KCN in ethanol
halogenoalkane heated with excess NH₃ in ethanol in a sealed tube
alkene heated with steam and H₃PO₄
pp.exp: NH₃ is a nucleophile; heating it in excess with ethanol under pressure gives RNH₂. KCN gives a nitrile, NaOH(aq) an alcohol, steam an alcohol.

pp.skill: Products of 1-bromobutane with different nucleophiles/bases
pp.mis: Thinking ethanolic NaOH gives an alcohol
pp.stem:
Three statements about 1-bromobutane are listed.
1 With hot KCN in ethanol it forms pentanenitrile.
2 With excess ethanolic NH₃, heated under pressure, it forms butylamine.
3 With hot NaOH in ethanol it forms mainly butan-1-ol.
Which are correct?
pp.exp: CN⁻ adds one carbon (pentanenitrile) and NH₃ gives C₄H₉NH₂. Hot ethanolic NaOH acts as a base, causing elimination to but-1-ene, not the alcohol.

pp.skill: Major product with hot ethanolic NaOH
pp.mis: Calling elimination a condensation
pp.stem: 2-bromo-2-methylbutane is heated under reflux with concentrated NaOH in ethanol. Which statement about the major type of reaction is correct?
pp.exp: OH⁻ in ethanol acts as a base: it removes H⁺ from a carbon next to C–Br while Br⁻ leaves, giving an alkene and HBr (as H₂O + Br⁻). This is elimination.

pp.skill: Choosing a reagent for the best alkene yield
pp.mis: Choosing aqueous KOH
pp.stem: 1-bromobutane is to be turned into but-1-ene in as high a yield as possible. Which should be used?
opts: excess NH₃ in a sealed tube
pp.exp: Ethanol as solvent and heat favour elimination. In water, OH⁻ mainly substitutes; NH₃ and CN⁻ substitute too.

pp.skill: Formula of an elimination product
pp.mis: Keeping the oxygen of the hydroxide in the product
pp.stem: 1-bromobutane is heated with ethanolic KOH. What is the molecular formula of the organic product?
pp.exp: HBr is removed from C₄H₉Br, leaving the alkene C₄H₈ (but-1-ene). C₄H₁₀O would be the substitution product.

pp.skill: Possible alkenes from elimination
pp.mis: Forgetting that H can be lost from either side
pp.stem: What are the possible elimination products (ignore stereoisomers) when 2-bromopentane is heated with KOH in ethanol?
pp.exp: H can be removed from C1 (giving pent-1-ene) or from C3 (giving pent-2-ene). Losing only one HBr cannot form a diene.

pp.skill: Counting elimination products including stereoisomers
pp.mis: Counting pent-2-ene once
pp.stem: Structural and stereoisomerism should be considered. 3-bromopentane is heated with concentrated NaOH in ethanol. How many isomeric organic products with formula C₅H₁₀ are formed?
pp.exp: Losing H from C2 or from C4 gives the same structure, pent-2-ene. Pent-2-ene has E and Z isomers, so there are 2 products.

pp.skill: Identifying halogenoalkanes from the number of alkenes
pp.mis: Forgetting E/Z isomers
pp.stem: Structural and stereoisomerism should be considered. X and Y both have formula C₅H₁₁Br. With hot ethanolic NaOH, X gives three isomeric alkenes and Y gives only one. What could X and Y be?
pp.exp: 2-bromopentane → pent-1-ene + E- and Z-pent-2-ene (3). 1-bromopentane → pent-1-ene only (1). 3-bromopentane gives 2; 2-bromo-2-methylbutane gives 2; (CH₃)₂CHCHBrCH₃ gives 2.

pp.skill: Products from a mixture of isomeric halogenoalkanes
pp.mis: Expecting two alkenes from two starting compounds
pp.stem: Include any stereoisomers. Some 1-bromopropane and some 2-bromopropane are mixed and refluxed with plenty of ethanolic NaOH. How many organic compounds result?
pp.exp: Both lose HBr to give CH₂=CHCH₃. Propene has no E/Z isomers (C1 carries two H atoms), so there is only one product.

pp.skill: Isomers from a double elimination
pp.mis: Missing the E/Z combinations
pp.stem: Structural and stereoisomerism should be considered. 2,6-dibromoheptane is heated under reflux with ethanolic KOH so that both Br atoms are eliminated. How many isomeric compounds with formula C₇H₁₂ are formed?
pp.exp: Each end can form C1=C2 (no E/Z) or C2=C3 (E or Z). Both terminal: hepta-1,6-diene (1). One of each: hepta-1,5-diene, E or Z (2). Both internal: hepta-2,5-diene EE, EZ, ZZ (3; EZ = ZE by symmetry). Total 6.

pp.skill: Mr of the product of a double elimination
pp.mis: Stopping after one elimination or substituting
pp.stem: 1,5-dibromopentane is heated with an excess of ethanolic NaOH until no further reaction occurs. What is the Mr of the major organic product?
pp.exp: Two HBr are lost: CH₂=CHCH₂CH=CH₂ (penta-1,4-diene), C₅H₈, Mr = 5(12.0) + 8(1.0) = 68. 104 would be pentane-1,5-diol from substitution.

pp.skill: Drawing the SN1 mechanism and explaining a rate change
pp.stem: Ethanol reacts with sodium to give ethoxide ions, CH₃CH₂O⁻. These react with 2-bromo-2-methylpropane to give an ether, (CH₃)₃C–O–CH₂CH₃.

parts.q: Write an equation for the reaction of ethanol with sodium.
The reaction of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane with ethoxide follows an SN1 mechanism. Describe the mechanism, including charges, dipoles, lone pairs and curly arrows.
ms: C–Br dipole (δ+ C, δ− Br); curly arrow from the C–Br bond to Br
curly arrow from a lone pair on the O of CH₃CH₂O⁻ to C⁺, giving the ether

parts.q: State and explain how the rate would change if 2-chloro-2-methylpropane were used instead.
ms: the C–Cl bond is stronger than C–Br, so the slow step (C–X breaking) is harder / higher activation energy

parts.q: Explain why 2-bromo-2-methylpropane reacts by SN1 rather than SN2.
ms: the tertiary carbocation is stabilised by three electron-donating alkyl groups (and the bulky groups hinder attack on the carbon)
